title: Void Ending in an Opposition to Uranus
source: Picatrix (adapted), Book I chapter 5, Book II chapter 3 and Book III chapter 1

<!-- generated by tools/content/gen-void.ts; edit the generator, not this file -->

The opposition is the hardest figure the Moon can close on: the text grades it as extreme enmity, because the signs it joins stand opposed across all four natural qualities. It shares with the square the warnings that guard every election, and a Moon waning in light and faced by Saturn is the source's own example of a serious misfortune.

When the Moon closes her course in a sign with an opposition to Uranus, the quiet stretch that follows carries something of his cold, sky-borne surprises. Uranus is nowhere in Picatrix: the planet was found with a telescope in 1781, some seven centuries after the book was written, and no passage of the source speaks of it. What follows is this almanac's extension of Picatrix's doctrine, never the medieval text's own words. Named for the Greek god of the sky, it is read here as a cold, far, sky-colored planet of upheaval, so that a course closing on it ends on a surprise rather than a settled end.
